questions.q: Name the three nutrients mentioned that are essential for supporting the rapid growth of muscles, bones, and blood during adolescence.
questions.a: The three nutrients are protein (for muscle and tissue), calcium (for bones), and iron (for blood). A wrong answer suggests the student has not grasped the basic role of these specific nutrients in physical development.

questions.q: If an adolescent eats only one type of food, like only carbohydrates, why might they struggle with their physical growth?
questions.a: Because growth requires building blocks like protein and minerals (calcium/iron) which a single-source diet lacks, leading to incomplete development. A wrong answer shows a misunderstanding of the need for a "varied" diet.

questions.q: How does regular physical exercise interact with a healthy diet during the adolescent growth spurt?
questions.a: Exercise uses the nutrients consumed to strengthen muscles and bones, while the diet provides the energy and materials for that exercise. A wrong answer indicates the student views diet and exercise as unrelated activities rather than a combined system.

questions.q: Why is iron intake particularly emphasized for females during the adolescent years?
questions.a: Iron is essential for replacing blood lost during menstruation and for maintaining the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood. A wrong answer suggests a lack of awareness regarding biological changes during adolescence.

questions.q: Is it better to consume a single "superfood" supplement or a varied diet of whole grains, pulses, and vegetables? Justify your answer.
questions.a: A varied diet is better because it provides a balance of all necessary nutrients, not just one. A wrong answer suggests a misunderstanding of how complex physical growth requires a range of different substances simultaneously.

questions.q: Design a simple plan for your school week that includes both nutritional variety and physical activity. What are your priorities?
questions.a: The plan should include balanced meals (grains, protein, fruits/veg) and daily movement (sports, walking, or play). A poor answer fails to connect the food consumed to the energy/growth needed for the activities mentioned.
